title: Getting the photon out: waveguides, facets, cavities

slides.title: Getting the Photon Out: Waveguides, Facets, Cavities
slides.subtitle: Section 4: Photonic Extraction and Waveguide Engineering
slides.notes: Welcome to Section 4 of our lecture series. In previous sections, we analyzed carrier injection, capture dynamics, and radiative recombination in quantum dots. However, creating a single exciton photon inside a high-index semiconductor chip is only half the battle: extracting that photon into a usable optical mode presents an immense electromagnetic challenge. Because semiconductors like gallium arsenide and indium phosphide possess large refractive indices near 3.5, total internal reflection traps more than 97.9% of generated light within the planar substrate. Without dedicated photonic engineering, the extraction efficiency of an unpatterned surface emitter is approximately 2%. In this section, we develop the electromagnetic formalism for guiding, shaping, and collecting single photons using edge-emitting ridge waveguides. We will trace the transverse resonance equations of dielectric slabs, solve 2D ridge profiles with the effective-index method, examine spontaneous emission enhancement via the beta factor, and analyze group index dispersion. Furthermore, we will quantify mirror reflection at cleaved facets, exponential propagation loss, and Gaussian far-field numerical aperture collection. By combining these mechanisms, we establish the multiplicative extraction chain modeled in our simulator and explain why high-reflectivity coatings, short cavities, and high-numerical-aperture optics are essential to achieve single-photon detection at room temperature [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 1, 7] [Chuang (2009) ch. 7].

slides.title: Surface vs Edge Emission: The Total Internal Reflection Barrier
bullets: High semiconductor index ($n \approx 3.5$) establishes narrow critical angle $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/n) \approx 16.6^\circ$.
Escape cone subtends solid angle $\Omega = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_c) \approx \pi / n^2$ steradians.
Planar surface extraction is limited to $\eta_{surf} = (1 - \cos\theta_c)/2 \approx 2.08\%$ (paraxial $2.04\%$).
Over 97.9% of generated photons remain trapped in unguided substrate and planar modes.
In-plane edge waveguides channel emitted photons directly along monolithic integrated circuits on-chip.
Waveguide routing eliminates vertical collection lenses and enables scalable planar photonic systems.

equations.caption: exact extraction efficiency into one half-space for refractive index $n=3.5$, critical angle $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/n)$, and paraxial approximation

figure.caption: Total internal reflection escape cone for planar surface emission versus in-plane waveguide guiding.

slides.notes: A fundamental hurdle in semiconductor optoelectronics is the high refractive index of III-V materials. For indium phosphide and gallium arsenide, the refractive index at near-infrared wavelengths is approximately 3.5. Applying Snell's law at a planar semiconductor-air boundary yields an escape critical angle of only 16.6 degrees. Light emitted by an isotropic dipole outside this narrow cone undergoes total internal reflection at the semiconductor-air boundary. Integrating over the spherical escape cone into one half-space gives a solid angle of approximately pi divided by n squared steradians. Relative to the full four-pi sphere, the exact extraction fraction is one minus cosine theta_c divided by two, which evaluates to 2.08%, closely approximated by the paraxial form one over four n squared as 2.04%. That means over 97.9% of generated photons are trapped in guided substrate modes or absorbed by contacts and substrates [Chuang (2009) ch. 7]. While vertical microcavities or surface micropillars can overcome this limit by redirecting light out of the wafer plane, they require complex epitaxial distributed Bragg reflectors and expensive macroscopic collection optics. By contrast, edge emission embraces total internal reflection: it embeds the quantum dot within a waveguiding core that routes light laterally across the chip. This in-plane architecture couples directly to on-chip optical waveguides, multiplexers, and integrated detectors, making it exceptionally attractive for scalable planar photonic integrated circuits [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 1].

slides.title: Dielectric Slab Waveguide: Transverse Resonance and Bound Modes
bullets: Vertical heterostructure confines light via refractive index contrast: $n_{core} > n_{clad}$.
Transverse wavevector $k_z = k_0\sqrt{n_{core}^2 - n_{eff}^2}$ and cladding decay $\gamma = k_0\sqrt{n_{eff}^2 - n_{clad}^2}$.
Transverse resonance condition for TE modes: $k_z d_{core} - 2\arctan(\gamma/k_z) = m\pi$.
Symmetric 296 nm / 3.22 / 3.05 slab root $n_{eff} = 3.154886$ matches `waveguide.slab_modes` (3.154888).
HKUST heterostructure: 296 nm core yields fundamental TE mode $n_{eff} = 3.1606$ at 668 nm.
Dot layer confinement factor $\Gamma_{dot} = 0.0074$ (0.74%) within the 2 nm active sheet.

equations.latex: k_z d_{core} - 2 \arctan\left(\frac{\gamma}{k_z}\right) = m \pi, \quad k_z = k_0\sqrt{n_{core}^2 - n_{eff}^2}, \; \gamma = k_0\sqrt{n_{eff}^2 - n_{clad}^2}
equations.caption: TE slab transverse resonance condition for core thickness $d_{core}$, vacuum wavenumber $k_0 = 2\pi/\lambda$, mode order $m$

figure.caption: Vertical refractive index profile and bound TE slab mode intensity $|E(z)|^2$ for the HKUST ridge stack at 668 nm.

slides.notes: To confine light in the vertical direction, we introduce an epitaxial dielectric slab waveguide consisting of a high-index core sandwiched between lower-index claddings. A self-consistent bound optical mode forms when a plane wave reflecting between the upper and lower interfaces reproduces its phase after one complete round trip. This transverse resonance requirement equates the round-trip transverse phase accumulation, two k_z d_core, minus the reflection phase shifts at the two cladding boundaries, two phi_clad, to an integer multiple of two pi. Because each reflection phase shift for transverse electric polarization is two arctan(gamma / k_z), the phase matching condition simplifies to k_z d_core minus two arctan(gamma / k_z) equals m pi. The eigenvalue of this transcendental equation determines the mode effective index n_eff. For a symmetric 296 nm slab with core index 3.22 and cladding 3.05 at 668 nm, this condition yields n_eff of 3.154886, reproducing our finite-difference solver waveguide.slab_modes (3.154888). In our simulator's fsim_core.waveguide module, the multilayer slab eigenproblem is solved numerically on a fine tridiagonal grid. For the complete HKUST heterostructure at 668 nm, the AlGaInP core clad by AlInP supports a fundamental TE mode with n_eff equal to 3.1606 and an active dot layer confinement factor Gamma_dot of 0.74% [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 7] [Chuang (2009) ch. 7].

slides.title: Ridge Waveguide: 2D Confinement and Effective-Index Method
bullets: Lateral confinement is formed by etching through cladding outside a 2000 nm ridge stripe.
Effective-index method separates the 2D Helmholtz equation into sequential 1D slab solves.
Vertical solve yields $n_{ridge} = 3.1606$ under the ridge; etched exterior falls back to $n_{outside} = 3.0500$ [A].
Lateral slab solve using $(n_{ridge}, n_{outside})$ gives 2D modal effective index $n_{eff} = 3.1571$.
Separable mode area $A_{mode} = \pi w_x w_y = 0.5874\ \mu\text{m}^2$ for the HKUST ridge.
Gaussian-equivalent $1/e^2$ beam radii: $w_x = 0.851\ \mu\text{m}$ (lateral) and $w_y = 0.220\ \mu\text{m}$ (vertical).

equations.latex: A_{mode} = \frac{\left(\int |E|^2 dx dy\right)^2}{\int |E|^4 dx dy} = w_{x,eff} \cdot w_{y,eff} = \pi w_x w_y
equations.caption: separable intensity effective mode area $A_{mode}$ and Gaussian $1/e^2$ beam waist radii $w_x, w_y$ ($A_{mode} = \pi w_x w_y$)

figure.caption: 2D optical mode intensity profile $|E(x,y)|^2$ reconstructed via separable effective-index method for a 2 um ridge.

slides.notes: Planar slab waveguides confine light vertically, but allowing photons to spread laterally would dilute intensity and ruin single-mode fiber coupling. To achieve two-dimensional confinement, a ridge waveguide is fabricated by lithographically defining a stripe, typically 2 microns wide, and etching away the cladding outside the stripe. Solving the full vector 2D Helmholtz equation analytically is intractable, so we employ the effective-index method [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 7]. We first solve the vertical 1D slab eigenproblem in the unetched central region to obtain the ridge effective index n_ridge of 3.1606. In the etched exterior, a 1200 nm etch removes the upper cladding, the upper core, and the well/dot sheet, plus 48 nm of the lower core; because the remaining stack cannot support a bound mode, waveguide.py uses an engineering fallback [A] to the cladding index n_outside of 3.0500. Next, we solve a lateral 1D slab with core index n_ridge and cladding n_outside, yielding the 2D effective index n_eff of 3.1571. Under separability, the mode area A_mode is the product of lateral and vertical intensity effective widths, which rigorously equals pi times w_x times w_y for Gaussian-equivalent 1/e^2 intensity radii. For this HKUST ridge at 668 nm, this produces A_mode of 0.5874 square microns, with w_x of 0.851 microns and w_y of 0.220 microns. For comparison, our fallback GaInP design at 770 nm yields A_mode of 0.5124 square microns with w_x of 0.830 microns and w_y of 0.197 microns [Chuang (2009) ch. 7].

slides.title: Guided Spontaneous Emission: Purcell Factor $F_{wg}$ and $\beta$
bullets: Guided mode continuum enhances spontaneous emission via 1D local density of states (LDOS).
Waveguide Purcell factor: $F_{wg} = \frac{3}{4\pi}\left(\frac{\lambda}{n_{dot}}\right)^2 \frac{n_g/n_{dot}}{A_{mode}} \xi_{pos}$.
Spontaneous emission coupling factor $\beta = F_{wg} / (1 + F_{wg})$ governs guided fraction.
Photonic-crystal waveguides report $\beta$ above 98% (Arcari 2014); a different guiding mechanism.
Fallback 2 um ridge waveguide provides $\beta = 0.0297$ (2.97%) with $F_{wg} = 0.0306$ at 770 nm.
Position factor $\xi_{pos} = |E(z_{dot})|^2 / \max|E|^2 > 0.95$ when dots sit at the vertical antinode.

equations.caption: Lecamp 2007 guided Purcell factor $F_{wg}$ and coupling factor $\beta$, position overlap $\xi_{pos} = |E(z_{dot})|^2/\max|E|^2$

figure.caption: Spontaneous emission $\beta$ factor vs mode area $A_{mode}$ for different group indices $n_g$, comparing ridge waveguides to photonic crystals.

slides.notes: When a quantum dot dipole radiates inside a structured dielectric waveguide, its spontaneous emission rate is modified according to Fermi's golden rule. Following the derivation by Lecamp, Lalanne, and Hugonin [PRL 99, 023902 (2007)], the spontaneous emission rate into the guided mode continuum is proportional to the one-dimensional local density of optical states. Normalizing this rate to the bulk spontaneous emission rate yields the waveguide Purcell factor F_wg. In this formula, the mode area A_mode appears in the denominator, while the group index n_g appears in the numerator. The spontaneous emission beta factor is the ratio of emission into the guided mode pair to total emission, F_wg divided by one plus F_wg. Photonic crystal waveguides are a different guiding mechanism: Arcari et al. [PRL 113, 093603 (2014)] report a photonic-crystal waveguide with beta above 98 percent, achieved without the ridge-waveguide geometry modeled here. In contrast, a standard 2-micron wide dielectric ridge waveguide has a larger mode area of 0.5046 square microns and a moderate group index of 4.358. With the InP dot refractive index of 3.418 at 770 nm from materials.refractive_index, this yields F_wg equal to 0.0306 and a beta factor of 2.97%. Furthermore, the position factor xi_pos accounts for dipole placement relative to the optical antinode, exceeding 0.95 at the core center [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 7].

slides.title: Waveguide Dispersion: Effective Index vs Group Index $n_g$
bullets: Group velocity $v_g = d\omega/dk$ governs packet propagation and local optical density of states.
Group index $n_g = c/v_g = n_{eff} - \lambda \frac{dn_{eff}}{d\lambda} = n_{eff} + \omega \frac{dn_{eff}}{d\omega}$.
Material chromatic dispersion ($dn_{mat}/d\lambda$) strongly dominates over geometric waveguide dispersion.
Finite difference in `waveguide.py` yields $n_g = 4.358$ vs $n_{eff} = 3.251$ at 770 nm (+34% boost).
Neglecting dispersion ($n_g = n_{eff}$) undercounts the guided Purcell factor by 25% ($0.746\times$).
Model caveat: $n_g$ rests on [E] ratio-scaled 700-850 nm material indices in `materials.py`.

equations.caption: group index $n_g$ combining phase index $n_{eff}$ and chromatic dispersion slope at wavelength $\lambda$

figure.caption: Effective index $n_{eff}(\lambda)$ and group index $n_g(\lambda)$ across 700-800 nm, highlighting the LDOS enhancement.

slides.notes: In waveguide quantum electrodynamics, the phase velocity c over n_eff dictates wavefront spacing, but energy transport and the local optical density of states are governed by the group velocity v_g equal to d omega by d k. Correspondingly, the group index n_g equals c divided by v_g, which can be expressed as n_eff minus lambda times d n_eff by d lambda. Waveguide dispersion combines geometric modal boundary conditions with material chromatic dispersion. In direct-bandgap III-V semiconductors operating near their band edge, material dispersion dominates: the refractive index rises sharply toward shorter wavelengths, so d n by d lambda is negative and large [Chuang (2009) ch. 7]. In our implementation within fsim_core.waveguide, n_g is computed using a 5 nm central finite difference on wavelength-aware layers. For our fallback GaInP ridge design at 770 nm, this calculation yields an effective index n_eff of 3.251, but a group index n_g of 4.358. This represents a 34.0% increase in group index over phase index. Crucially, omitting dispersion and assuming n_g equals n_eff would underestimate the guided Purcell factor by 25.4% (a 0.746x factor), directly undercounting the beta coupling factor. We must emphasize an important modeling caveat: because published optical tabulations are sparse, the 700 to 850 nm refractive indices for our phosphide alloys rest on [E] ratio-scaled models anchored to GaInP Schubert data [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 7].

slides.title: Facet Transmission: Breaking Symmetry with High-Reflectivity Mirrors
bullets: Cleaved semiconductor facet has normal Fresnel transmission $T_f = 1 - ((n_{eff}-1)/(n_{eff}+1))^2$.
For $n_{eff} = 3.253$, power reflection is $R_f = 28.06\%$ and raw transmission is $T_f = 71.94\%$.
Uncoated bare facet ($R_{back}=$None$\to R_{back}=R_f=28.06\%$): mid-ridge ray series gives $\eta_{facet} = 44.91\%$.
High-reflectivity (HR) back-facet coating ($R_{back} = 0.95$) redirects backward light forward.
Front-facet escape: mid-ridge ray series gives $\eta_{facet} = 78.39\%$ [DR]; Coldren $F_1$ gives $96.36\%$ (different quantities).
HR mirror provides a $1.75\times$ out-coupling boost over the bare, uncoated cleaved facet.

equations.latex: T_f = 1 - \left(\frac{n_{eff}-1}{n_{eff}+1}\right)^2, \quad \eta_{facet} = \frac{0.5\,T_f\,e^{-\alpha L/2}\,(1 + R_{back}\,e^{-\alpha L})}{1 - R_{back}\,R_f\,e^{-2\alpha L}}, \quad F_1 = \frac{(1-R_1)\sqrt{R_2}}{(1-R_1)\sqrt{R_2} + (1-R_2)\sqrt{R_1}}
equations.caption: Fresnel transmission $T_f$, mid-ridge ray-probability escape fraction $\eta_{facet}$ [DR] ($R_f=1-T_f$, single-pass propagation already folded in), and Coldren & Corzine front fraction $F_1$

figure.caption: Front facet extraction factor $\eta_{facet}$ as a function of back-facet reflectivity $R_{back}$, comparing the mid-ridge ray-series escape fraction and Coldren & Corzine F1 models.

slides.notes: Once a photon couples into the guided mode, it travels toward the cleaved facets terminating the waveguide. At normal incidence, the step between effective index n_eff of 3.253 and air produces a Fresnel power reflectivity of 28.06% and transmission T_f of 71.94%. Our simulator's current facet model is a ray-probability series with the dot placed at mid-ridge: the forward half of the emission travels half the cavity length and either escapes with probability T_f or reflects, the backward half reflects off the back facet with reflectivity R_back and travels the full cavity length forward, and the two paths sum over every round trip, with single-pass propagation loss already folded in, tagged [DR] in fsim_core.waveguide, after Coldren, Corzine and Masanovic ch. 2. An uncoated, bare cleaved back facet carries no coating at all, so R_back resolves to the same Fresnel reflectivity as the front, R_back equals R_f equals 28.06%, giving eta_facet of 44.91%. Depositing a dielectric high-reflectivity mirror coating with R_back of 0.95 on the rear facet raises this to 78.39%, a 1.75x boost. We must note this ray-series value is not the same quantity as Coldren and Corzine's lasing-cavity front-facet output-coupling fraction F1, which for the same R_back evaluates to 96.36%: F1 describes power output coupling from an active lasing cavity, while eta_facet is a spontaneous-emission escape probability, and the two are close but not interchangeable [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 2, mirror loss and facet reflectivity].
sources: Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 2, mirror loss and facet reflectivity

slides.title: Propagation Loss: Cavity Length Trade-off ($250\ \mu\text{m}$ vs $500\ \mu\text{m}$)
bullets: Internal waveguide attenuation follows exponential decay: $\eta_{prop} = \exp(-\alpha L)$.
Ridge scattering and free-carrier absorption give class loss $\alpha \approx 5\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ [E].
Long cavity ($L = 500\ \mu\text{m}$) suffers 22.1% loss: $\eta_{prop} = \exp(-5 \times 0.05) = 0.7788$.
Short cavity ($L = 250\ \mu\text{m}$) reduces loss to 11.8%: $\eta_{prop} = \exp(-5 \times 0.025) = 0.8825$.
Shortening cavity from 500 to 250 um delivers a $1.133\times$ throughput brightness advantage.
Lower bound on cavity length is limited by bar-cleaving yield, contact area, and thermal resistance.

equations.caption: optical power transmission over cavity length $L$ with linear attenuation coefficient $\alpha = 5\ \text{cm}^{-1}$

figure.caption: Waveguide transmission $\eta_{prop}$ vs cavity length $L$ and qualitative engineering trade-offs comparing 250 um and 500 um bars.

slides.notes: As photons traverse the optical waveguide between the quantum dot and the exit facet, they experience attenuation described by the Beer-Lambert law, eta_prop equals exponential of minus alpha times length L. In semiconductor ridge waveguides, the attenuation coefficient alpha arises primarily from sidewall roughness scattering and free-carrier absorption within doped cladding layers. For high-quality dry-etched III-V stripes, alpha is estimated around 5 inverse centimeters [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 7]. Over a standard laser cavity length of 500 microns, the optical attenuation factor alpha times L equals 0.25, giving an internal transmission of 77.88%. Shortening the cavity bar to 250 microns reduces alpha times L to 0.125, elevating the internal transmission to 88.25%. This 13.3% throughput gain represents a direct, linear improvement in detected photon count rate. However, cavity length cannot be made arbitrarily small in practice. Cleaving individual semiconductor bars shorter than 200 microns results in severe edge chipping and handling loss during packaging. Furthermore, halving cavity length halves electrical contact area, doubling series resistance and exacerbating local Joule heating. The 250 micron length selected in our acceptance sweep balances internal transmission against mechanical cleaving yield and electrical thermal dissipation [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 1].

slides.title: Far-Field Emission and Numerical Aperture (NA) Collection
bullets: Sub-micron facet emits an astigmatic Gaussian beam: $w_x = 0.828\ \mu\text{m}$ and $w_y = 0.194\ \mu\text{m}$.
Paraxial divergence half-angles: $\theta_{x,div} = \lambda/(\pi w_x) = 17.0^\circ$ and $\theta_{y,div} = \lambda/(\pi w_y) = 72.4^\circ$.
Symmetric circular cone collection $\eta_{circ} = 1 - \exp(-2\theta_{\max}^2/\theta_{div}^2)$ with $\theta_{\max} = \arcsin(\mathrm{NA})$.
Elliptical mode is integrated numerically in `waveguide.na_collection` (erf-product is square approximation).
New repository collection: $\mathrm{NA}=0.50$ captures $57.17\%$; $\mathrm{NA}=0.75$ captures $81.36\%$ (card default).
High $\mathrm{NA}=0.80$ captures $\eta_{NA} = 85.26\%$ [DR], a vital $1.491\times$ boost over NA 0.50.

equations.caption: paraxial $1/e^2$ divergence half-angles, circular-cone collection; elliptical modes integrated numerically, square-aperture erf-product approximation

figure.caption: Astigmatic far-field intensity radiation pattern and circular-cone collection efficiency $\eta_{NA}$ vs lens numerical aperture $\mathrm{NA}$.

slides.notes: Photons exiting the cleaved front facet diffract into free space as an astigmatic Gaussian beam. Because the waveguide mode has asymmetric dimensions, with Gaussian-equivalent 1/e^2 intensity radii w_x of 0.828 microns and w_y of 0.194 microns, diffraction angles differ between the two axes. Using the consistent paraxial divergence half-angle definition theta_div equals lambda over pi w_0, the lateral divergence half-angle theta_x is 17.0 degrees, while tight vertical sub-micron confinement produces rapid diffraction with theta_y of 72.4 degrees. An external microscope objective captures light within an acceptance cone theta_max equal to arcsin(NA). For a circular numerical aperture, a symmetric beam yields an analytical collection fraction of one minus exponential of minus two theta max squared over theta_div squared. For our elliptical mode, fsim_core.waveguide.na_collection evaluates the circular cone integral numerically using Gauss-Legendre quadrature. The legacy formula, an erf product, represented a square-aperture approximation that underestimated collection. With the corrected circular physics, a standard objective with NA of 0.50 captures 57.17% of emitted light. Our design card default NA of 0.75 captures 81.36%, while an NA of 0.80 collects 85.26%. Upgrading from NA 0.50 to 0.80 provides a vital 1.491x flux boost [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 7] [Saleh & Teich, Fundamentals of Photonics, Gaussian beam optics].

slides.title: Cavities as Context: Purcell Boost, Micropillars, and Lemma 1
bullets: Cavity Purcell factor $F_P = \frac{3}{4\pi^2} \left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^3 \frac{Q}{V_{mode}}$ boosts radiative rate $\Gamma_{rad} = F_P \Gamma_0$.
Planar DBR cavities offer $F_P \sim 1-3$; etched micropillars achieve $F_P \sim 5-25$; PhC cavities exceed 100.
Simulator's `cavity` block models vertical DBR planar filtering and resonant enhancement $G$.
For edge designs, `cavity.enabled` is explicitly set to `false` in device design cards.
Lemma 1: collection efficiency affects brightness, never intrinsic $g^{(2)}(0)$ (except via spectral leakage $\varepsilon$).
Coexistence of edge waveguides and resonant vertical cavities lacks consistent leakage accounting.

equations.caption: Purcell factor $F_P$ for quality factor $Q$ and mode volume $V_{mode}$; invariance of $g^{(2)}(0)$ under linear loss (Lemma 1)

figure.caption: Comparison of optical architectures and Lemma 1 invariance of quantum correlation $g^{(2)}(0)$ under linear collection loss.

slides.notes: It is instructive to place ridge waveguides in the broader context of optical microcavities. In cavity quantum electrodynamics, the Purcell factor F_P scales with the cavity quality factor Q divided by effective mode volume V_mode. Resonant microcavities, such as planar DBRs, etched micropillars, and photonic crystal defects, enhance the spontaneous emission rate and funnel emission into a single spatial mode [Fox (2006) ch. 8]. In our simulation architecture, the cavity block models vertical DBR microcavity filtering and Purcell enhancement G. However, for edge-emitting designs, cavity.enabled is explicitly disabled. There are two decisive physical reasons for this. First, our platform contract formalizes Lemma 1 (docs/rt_edge_contract.md): linear out-coupling and collection efficiency scale detected photon brightness, but they never alter intrinsic multiphoton purity g2(0), except through the existing spectral-leakage epsilon path. A lossy linear channel acts as a random Bernoulli beamsplitter: because coincidence counts and single-photon counts scale with the exact same power of collection efficiency, normalized g2(0) is strictly invariant under linear loss. The multiphoton purity is determined by dot loading, spectral overlap epsilon, and background fraction rho via g2 equals one minus rho squared into one minus epsilon. Second, device.evaluate() itself raises on this combination: emission.type='edge' with cavity.enabled has no supported cavity-leakage accounting in this tier, a compatibility guard [A] in fsim_core.device, not a published result [docs/rt_edge_contract.md].

slides.title: The Complete Extraction Chain: Sub-Factor Decomposition
bullets: Total edge out-coupling decomposes multiplicatively: $\eta_{total} = \beta \cdot \eta_{facet} \cdot \eta_{NA}$ ($\eta_{facet}$ already includes propagation).
Favorable NA=0.80: $\beta = 2.97\%$, $\eta_{facet} = 78.40\%$ (mid-ridge ray series), $\eta_{NA} = 85.3\% \implies \eta_{total} = 1.99\%$.
HR mirror lever ($R_{back} = 0.95$ vs bare facet $R_{back}=R_f=0.28$): a $1.75\times$ facet-escape multiplier.
Cavity length lever ($L=250$ vs $500\ \mu\text{m}$): ray-series gain is $1.190\times$, not the naive $1.133\times$ ratio.
Objective collection lever ($\mathrm{NA} = 0.80$ vs $0.50$): captures circular cone diffraction, adding $1.485\times$ gain.
Combined levers provide a $3.08\times$ boost (facet, cavity, NA) -- still far below the 1000 counts/s floor.

slides.notes: We are now in a position to assemble the complete optical out-coupling chain. The current facet model, fsim_core.waveguide.facet_escape_fraction, already folds single-pass ridge propagation into eta_facet, so eta_total decomposes into three independent physical factors, not four: the spontaneous emission beta factor of 0.02970, the mid-ridge ray-series facet factor of 0.78402 under a 95% rear mirror (resolved LIVE from the card via _resolve_edge, not a stale hardcoded n_eff), and the circular numerical aperture collection efficiency of 0.85262 with an NA 0.80 objective. Multiplying these gives an overall extraction efficiency of 1.985%. Coating the rear facet delivers a 1.75x gain over the bare, uncoated cleaved facet. The cavity-length lever's OWN ray-series ratio -- facet_escape_fraction at 250 versus 500 microns -- gives 1.190x, not the naive 1.133x pure-propagation ratio a bare Beer-Lambert exponential would suggest; combined with the 1.485x NA-collection gain and the 1.75x facet gain, the three design levers together provide a 3.08x combined gain. Under the corrected finite-pulse loading model, the collected flux this chain multiplies into is only 582.8 photons/s at the best sampled corner (NA=0.80: 80.3/s at this slide's own 300 K point before the lever sweep's other axes are applied, NA=0.75: 76.7/s, baseline: 21.8/s) -- the flux margin is 0.58, below the 1000 counts/s floor, so even this best sampled combination of design levers does not by itself restore eligibility [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 1, 2, 7].

slides.title: Section Summary: The Photonic Pathway from Dipole to Detector
bullets: Total internal reflection traps ~98% of light in unpatterned planar semiconductors.
Ridge waveguides guide in-plane emission into a single transverse mode ($A_{mode} \approx 0.51\ \mu\text{m}^2$).
Guided spontaneous emission factor $\beta \approx 2.97\%$ is modest but highly manufacturable.
Group index dispersion ($n_g = 4.36$) boosts guided LDOS by 34% (omission undercounts by 25%).
Rear HR coating ($R_{back} = 0.95$) and short cavity ($250\ \mu\text{m}$) maximize photon escape.
High-NA circular collection ($\mathrm{NA} = 0.80$, $\eta_{NA} = 85.3\%$) still leaves flux below the 1000 counts/s floor.
slides.notes: To summarize Section 4, getting single photons out of a semiconductor chip requires a disciplined, multi-stage engineering approach. Without waveguiding, high refractive index contrast traps nearly 98% of light in planar substrate modes. By fabricating a ridge waveguide, we channel emission into a bound optical mode with sub-micron dimensions. Although the resulting spontaneous emission coupling factor beta of 2.97% is modest compared to cryogenic photonic crystal cavities, edge-emitting ridge waveguides offer robust planar electrical injection, standard fabrication tolerances, and straightforward integration with on-chip optical circuitry. Material dispersion significantly enhances this coupling, as chromatic dispersion near the bandgap boosts the group index by 34%, enhancing the one-dimensional local density of states; omitting it undercounts coupling by 25%. Once guided, photons must be extracted efficiently: deposition of an HR coating on the rear facet breaks front-back symmetry to eliminate backward losses, while shortening cavity length to 250 microns minimizes material propagation absorption. Finally, high numerical aperture collection optics capture astigmatic far-field diffraction, delivering an end-to-end extraction efficiency of about 1.99% -- still short of the 1000 counts per second eligibility floor under the corrected loading model: the sweep's own verdict is FAIL (evidence incomplete, no eligible rows), headline coverage 0/768. In the next section, we will integrate this photonic extraction model with electrical transport and junction heating to evaluate full room-temperature single-photon device operation [Coldren, Corzine, Masanovic (2012) ch. 1, 7] [Chuang (2009) ch. 7] [Saleh & Teich, Fundamentals of Photonics, Gaussian beam optics] [Lecamp PRL 99, 023902 (2007)] [Arcari PRL 113, 093603 (2014)].
